149-also described below.)
150-
151-## Design
152-
153-Copying between regions in linear memory or a table is accomplished with the
154-new `*.copy` instructions:
155-
156-* `memory.copy`: copy from one region of linear memory to another
157:* `table.copy`: copy from one region of a table to another
158-
159-Filling a memory region can be accomplished with `memory.fill`:
160-
161-* `memory.fill`: fill a region of linear memory with a given byte value
162-
163-The [binary format for the data
164-section](https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/binary/modules.html#binary-datasec)
165-currently has a collection of segments, each of which has a memory index, an
166-initializer expression for its offset, and its raw data.
167-
168-Since WebAssembly currently does not allow for multiple memories, the memory
169-index of each segment must be zero. We can repurpose this 32-bit integer as a
170-flags field where new meaning is attached to nonzero values.
171-
172-When the low bit of the new flags field is `1`, this segment is _passive_. A
173-passive segment will not be automatically copied into the memory or table on
174-instantiation, and must instead be applied manually using the following new
175-instructions:
176-
177-* `memory.init`: copy a region from a data segment
178:* `table.init`: copy a region from an element segment
179-
180-A passive segment has no initializer expression, since it will be specified
181:as an operand to `memory.init` or `table.init`.
182-
183-Segments can also be shrunk to size zero by using the following new instructions:
184-
185-* `data.drop`: discard the data in an data segment
186-* `elem.drop`: discard the data in an element segment
187-
188-An active segment is equivalent to a passive segment, but with an implicit
189:`memory.init` followed by a `data.drop` (or `table.init` followed by a
190-`elem.drop`) that is prepended to the module's start function.
191-
192-Additionally, the reference-types proposal introduces the notion of a function
193-reference (a function whose address is a program value).  To support this,
194-element segments can have several encodings, and can also be used to
195-forward-declare functions whose address will be taken; see below.
196-
197-The reference-types proposal also introduces the bulk instructions `table.fill`
198-and `table.grow`, both of which take a function reference as an initializer
199-argument.
200-
201-### Data segments
202-
203-The meaning of the bits of the flag field (a `varuint32`) for data segments is:
204-
205-| Bit | Meaning                                        |
206-| -   | -                                              |
207-| 0   | 0=is active, 1=is passive                      |
208-| 1   | if bit 0 clear: 0=memory 0, 1=has memory index |
209-
210-which yields this view, with the fields carried by each flag value:
211-
212-| Flags | Meaning                  | Memory index | Offset in memory | Count       | Payload |
213-| -     | -                        | -            | -                | -           | -       |
214-| 0     | Active                   |              | `init_expr`      | `varuint32` | `u8`*   |
215-| 1     | Passive                  |              |                  | `varuint32` | `u8`*   |
216-| 2     | Active with memory index | `varuint32`  | `init_expr`      | `varuint32` | `u8`*   |
217-
218-All other flag values are illegal.  At present the memory index must be zero,
219-but the upcoming multi-memory proposal changes that.
220-
221-
222-### Element segments
223-
224-The meaning of the bits of the flag field (a `varuint32`) for element segments is:
225-
226-| Bit | Meaning                                          |
227-| -   | -                                                |
228-| 0   | 0=is active, 1=is passive                        |
229-| 1   | if bit 0 clear: 0=table 0, 1=has table index     | 
230-|     | if bit 0 set: 0=active, 1=declared               |
231-| 2   | 0=carries indices; 1=carries elemexprs          |
232-
233-which yields this view, with the fields carried by each flag value:
234-
235-| Flag | Meaning                          | Table index | Offset in table | Encoding      | Count       | Payload      |
236-| -    | -                                | -           | -               | -             | -           | -            |
237-| 0    | Legacy active, funcref externval |             | `init_expr`     |               | `varuint32` | `idx`*       |
238-| 1    | Passive, externval               |             |                 | `extern_kind` | `varuint32` | `idx`*       |
239-| 2    | Active, externval                | `varuint32` | `init_expr`     | `extern_kind` | `varuint32` | `idx`*       |
240-| 3    | Declared, externval              |             |                 | `extern_kind` | `varuint32` | `idx`*       |
241-| 4    | Legacy active, funcref elemexpr  |             | `init_expr`     |               | `varuint32` | `elem_expr`* |
242-| 5    | Passive, elemexpr                |             |                 | `elem_type`   | `varuint32` | `elem_expr`* |
243-| 6    | Active, elemexpr                 | `varuint32` | `init_expr`     | `elem_type`   | `varuint32` | `elem_expr`* |
244-| 7    | Declared, elemexpr               |             |                 | `elem_type`   | `varuint32` | `elem_expr`* |
245-
246-All other flag values are illegal.  Note that the "declared" attribute
247-is not used by this proposal, but is used by the reference-types
248-proposal.
249-
--
349-
350-A trap occurs if:
351-
352-* the destination offset plus size is greater than the length of the target memory
353-
354-The bounds check is performed before any data are written.
355-
356-
357:### `table.init`, `elem.drop`, and `table.copy` instructions
358-
359-The `table.*` instructions behave similarly to the `memory.*` instructions, with
360-the difference that they operate on element segments and tables, instead of
361:data segments and memories. The offset and length operands of `table.init` and
362:`table.copy` have element units instead of bytes as well.
363-
364-## Passive Segment Initialization Example
365-
366-Consider if there are two data sections, the first is always active and the
367-second is conditionally active if global 0 has a non-zero value. This could be
368-implemented as follows:
369-
370-```webassembly
371-(import "a" "global" (global i32))  ;; global 0
372-(memory 1)
373-(data (i32.const 0) "hello")   ;; data segment 0, is active so always copied
374-(data "goodbye")               ;; data segment 1, is passive
375-
376-(func $start
377-  (if (global.get 0)
378-
379-    ;; copy data segment 1 into memory 0 (the 0 is implicit)
380-    (memory.init 1
381-      (i32.const 16)    ;; target offset
382-      (i32.const 0)     ;; source offset
383-      (i32.const 7))    ;; length
384-
385-    ;; The memory used by this segment is no longer needed, so this segment can
386-    ;; be dropped.
387-    (data.drop 1))
388-)
389-(start $start)
390-```
391-
392-### Instruction encoding
393-
394-All bulk memory instructions are encoded as a 0xfc prefix byte, followed by
395-another opcode, optionally followed by more immediates:
396-
397-```
398-instr ::= ...
399-        | 0xfc operation:uint8 ...
400-```
401-
402-| Name | Opcode | Immediate | Description |
403-| ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- |
404-| `memory.init` | `0xfc 0x08` | `segment:varuint32`, `memory:0x00` | copy from a passive data segment to linear memory |
405-| `data.drop` | `0xfc 0x09` | `segment:varuint32` | prevent further use of passive data segment |
406-| `memory.copy` | `0xfc 0x0a` | `memory_dst:0x00` `memory_src:0x00` | copy from one region of linear memory to another region |
407-| `memory.fill` | `0xfc 0x0b` | `memory:0x00` | fill a region of linear memory with a given byte value |
408:| `table.init` | `0xfc 0x0c` | `segment:varuint32`, `table:0x00` | copy from a passive element segment to a table |
409-| `elem.drop` | `0xfc 0x0d` | `segment:varuint32` | prevent further use of a passive element segment |
410:| `table.copy` | `0xfc 0x0e` | `table_dst:0x00` `table_src:0x00` | copy from one region of a table to another region |
411-
412-### `DataCount` section
413-
414-The WebAssembly binary format is designed to be validated in a single pass. If
415-a section requires information to validate, it is guaranteed that this
416-information will be present in a previous section.
417-
418-The `memory.{init,drop}` instructions break this guarantee. Both of these
419-instructions are used in the `Code` section. They each have a data segment
420-index immediate, but the vector of data segments is not available until the
421-`Data` section is parsed, which occurs after the `Code` section.
422-
423-To keep single-pass validation, the number of data segments defined in the
424-`Data` section must be available before the `Code` section. This information is
425-provided in a new `DataCount` section with the code `12`.
426-
427-Like all sections, the `DataCount` section is optional. If present, it must
428-appear in the following order:
429-
430-| Section Name | Code | Description |
431-| ------------ | ---- | ----------- |
432-| Type | `1` | Function signature declarations |
433-| Import | `2` | Import declarations |
434-| Function | `3` | Function declarations |
435-| Table | `4` | Indirect function table and other tables |
436-| Memory | `5` | Memory attributes |
437-| Global | `6` | Global declarations |
438-| Export | `7` | Exports |
439-| Start | `8` | Start function declaration |
440-| Element | `9` | Elements section |
441-| DataCount | `12` | Data segment count |
442-| Code | `10` | Function bodies (code) |
443-| Data | `11` | Data segments |
444-
445-The `DataCount` section has just one field that specifies the number of data
446-segments in the `Data` section:
447-
448-| Field | Type | Description |
449-| ----- | ---- | ----------- |
450-| count | `varuint32` | count of data segments in `Data` section |
451-
452-The binary is malformed if `count` is not equal to the number of data segments
453-in the `Data` section. The binary is also malformed if the `DataCount` section
454-is omitted and a `memory.init` or `data.drop` instruction is used.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Exercise multi-megabyte decoding/lowering without involving LLVM code generation."""
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import time
ROOT=Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
OUT=ROOT/'tests/out'

def leb(n):
    b=bytearray()
    while n>=128:b.append((n&127)|128);n>>=7
    b.append(n)
    return bytes(b)
def section(tag,payload):return bytes([tag])+leb(len(payload))+payload

def main():
    OUT.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
    body=b'\0'+bytes([0x41,1,0x41,2,0x6a,0x1a])*300000+b'\x0b'
    data=bytes(range(256))*16384
    wasm=(b'\0asm\1\0\0\0'+section(1,b'\1\x60\0\0')+section(3,b'\1\0')+
          section(5,b'\1\0'+leb(64))+section(10,b'\1'+leb(len(body))+body)+
          section(11,b'\1\0\x41\0\x0b'+leb(len(data))+data))
    path=OUT/'stress.wasm';path.write_bytes(wasm)
    start=time.monotonic()
    subprocess.run([str(ROOT/'target/release/wasm2llvm'),str(path),'-o',str(OUT/'stress.ll')],check=True,timeout=60)
    elapsed=time.monotonic()-start
    print('stress: %d input bytes, %d output bytes, %.3f seconds'%(len(wasm),(OUT/'stress.ll').stat().st_size,elapsed))
if __name__=='__main__':main()

# wasm2llvm implementation notes

## Scope and design

The payloads require wasm32 MVP plus **multi-value, sign-extension operations,
nontrapping float-to-integer conversions, bulk memory, and SIMD 1.0**. All
instructions in those proposals are implemented, including all 236 SIMD
opcodes, bulk table operations, passive/declarative segments, start functions,
and multi-value block/loop parameters. Reference-type instructions, relaxed
SIMD, threads, exceptions, tail calls, memory64, multi-memory, GC, extended
constant expressions, and other proposals are rejected.

The translator is Rust/std only, with no Cargo dependencies. It reads its input,
validates it, generates textual LLVM, and writes the requested output; it has no
subprocess, tool-discovery, auxiliary-file, or network code.

* `parse.rs` implements bounded binary readers, exact LEB encodings and section
  structure; `validate.rs` checks types, control-stack polymorphism, indices,
  limits, initializers, memory alignments, and SIMD lanes, including dead code.
* `ir.rs` uses native typed functions and aggregate multi-results internally.
  Slot-ABI wrappers handle imports/exports. Operands are SSA values; entry-block
  allocas implement locals and structured-control merges, and are promoted by
  LLVM at optimization. Indirect calls use structural signature IDs.
* `simd.rs` lowers to vector arithmetic, comparisons, shuffles, extensions,
  narrowing, reductions, and LLVM intrinsics. Dynamic byte swizzle uses a
  portable vector selection network, without target-specific CPU requirements.
* Bounds and trap conditions are explicit. Signed division/remainder overflow,
  shift counts, floating conversion ranges/NaNs, and SIMD saturation are handled
  before potentially undefined LLVM operations. No fast-math/FMA flags are used.
* Linear memory reserves a lazy, anonymous 4 GiB mapping on x86-64 Linux. Logical
  size/max checks implement growth; untouched new pages are already zero. This
  is not a guard-page implementation: all wasm memory bounds are checked.
* A 30,000-call depth budget prevents optimized unbounded recursion from
  becoming an infinite native loop. ABI entries and the common trap path reset
  bookkeeping, so trapping does not poison subsequent calls. Native stack
  exhaustion remains possible for large frames, as permitted by the ABI.

## Limits and tradeoffs

Only function imports have an ABI here; nonfunction imports are rejected with
an explicit diagnostic. Declared locals are limited to 1,000,000 per function
to avoid compressed local declarations exhausting the translator. The generated
instance is single-threaded and has no teardown entry point (none is specified).
The portable swizzle network is less efficient than a CPU-specific byte-shuffle
instruction. There is no dedicated pre-LLVM optimizing pass or bounds-check
elimination pass; LLVM performs ordinary promotion/inlining/optimization.

## Tests run

All execution comparisons below were run against `w2l-ref`, with generated code
compiled by LLVM 23 at **both `-O0` and `-O2`**:

* `cargo build --release --offline` and all **11** Rust unit tests pass.
* `tests/test.py`: **16 differential runs / 1,370 comparisons**, including all
  payloads' codec encode/decode workflows, packet bytes/final ranges, multi-value,
  control flow, bulk memory/table operations, host imports, traps, trap recovery,
  and malformed/invalid/out-of-scope rejection.
* `tests/scalar_matrix.py`: **41,966 commands per optimization level**, covering
  every scalar numeric opcode, NaNs, signed zeros, division overflow, shifts,
  and trapping/saturating conversion boundaries; no mismatches.
* `tests/simd_matrix.py`: **9,291 commands per optimization level**, covering
  every SIMD 1.0 opcode, lane endpoints, memory boundaries, arithmetic extremes,
  NaNs, and random vector bit patterns; no mismatches.
* `tests/smith.py`: **400 deterministic generated modules** translated, compiled,
  and differentially executed at both optimization levels. Unsupported features
  are explicitly disabled and reference loading checks the actual scope.
* `tests/recursion.py`: finite 10,000-frame calls, direct/mutual unbounded
  recursion trapping with code 8, and successful calls after traps all pass.
* `tests/stress.py`: **5,994,351-byte** synthetic module translated to
  20,273,963 bytes of LLVM IR in **0.265 seconds** in this environment.

An additional combined clean-CARGO_HOME/empty-environment/syscall-trace check
was attempted but blocked by the session's command permissions; it was not run.
No hidden acceptance tests were available. See `tests/README.md` for commands.

# Local tests

All test programs are standard-library Python or C; external tools are used only
by tests, never by the translator.

```sh
cargo build --release --offline
cargo test --offline
python3 -I tests/test.py --no-build

mkdir -p tests/out
clang -std=c11 -O2 -rdynamic tests/harness.c -ldl -o tests/out/harness
python3 -I tests/scalar_matrix.py
python3 -I tests/simd_matrix.py tests/out/harness
python3 -I tests/recursion.py
python3 -I tests/smith.py --count 100
python3 -I tests/stress.py
```

`test.py` builds its own native driver and uses a temporary directory. Use
`--only control`, `--only bulk`, `--opt 0`, `--opt 2`, `--quick`, or `--keep`
to select work and preserve generated artifacts. The complete default run
includes all four payloads.

The other scripts preserve artifacts in ignored `tests/out/`. `smith.py` accepts
`--start N` and `--count N`; the recorded 400-module run used seeds 0 through 399.
Smith's unsupported features are explicitly disabled, and each generated module
is checked against the reference engine's scope before translation.

The C driver accepts the reference line protocol, with `.so` paths instead of
`.wasm` paths for `load`. It implements the provided imports and explicit trap
recovery. It does not install a native stack-overflow handler; recursion tests
use small frames and the translator's explicit depth trap.

Comparisons ignore unused ABI-slot bytes and allow NaN variation only for
arithmetic floating-point results. Integer results, bitwise operations, encoded
packets, and memory byte comparisons remain exact.

# wasm2llvm implementation notes

## Scope and design

The payloads require wasm32 MVP plus **multi-value, sign-extension operations,
nontrapping float-to-integer conversions, bulk memory, and SIMD 1.0**. All
instructions in those proposals are implemented, including all 236 SIMD
opcodes, bulk table operations, passive/declarative segments, start functions,
and multi-value block/loop parameters. Reference-type instructions, relaxed
SIMD, threads, exceptions, tail calls, memory64, multi-memory, GC, extended
constant expressions, and other proposals are rejected.

The translator is Rust/std only, with no Cargo dependencies. It reads its input,
validates it, generates textual LLVM, and writes the requested output; it has no
subprocess, tool-discovery, auxiliary-file, or network code.

* `parse.rs` implements bounded binary readers, exact LEB encodings and section
  structure; `validate.rs` checks types, control-stack polymorphism, indices,
  limits, initializers, memory alignments, and SIMD lanes, including dead code.
* `ir.rs` uses native typed functions and aggregate multi-results internally.
  Slot-ABI wrappers handle imports/exports. Operands are SSA values; entry-block
  allocas implement locals and structured-control merges, and are promoted by
  LLVM at optimization. Indirect calls use structural signature IDs.
* `simd.rs` lowers to vector arithmetic, comparisons, shuffles, extensions,
  narrowing, reductions, and LLVM intrinsics. Dynamic byte swizzle uses a
  portable vector selection network, without target-specific CPU requirements.
* Bounds and trap conditions are explicit. Signed division/remainder overflow,
  shift counts, floating conversion ranges/NaNs, and SIMD saturation are handled
  before potentially undefined LLVM operations. No fast-math/FMA flags are used.
* Linear memory reserves a lazy, anonymous 4 GiB mapping on x86-64 Linux. Logical
  size/max checks implement growth; untouched new pages are already zero. This
  is not a guard-page implementation: all wasm memory bounds are checked.
* A 30,000-call depth budget prevents optimized unbounded recursion from
  becoming an infinite native loop. ABI entries and the common trap path reset
  bookkeeping, so trapping does not poison subsequent calls. Native stack
  exhaustion remains possible for large frames, as permitted by the ABI.

## Limits and tradeoffs

Only function imports have an ABI here; nonfunction imports are rejected with
an explicit diagnostic. Declared locals are limited to 1,000,000 per function
to avoid compressed local declarations exhausting the translator. The generated
instance is single-threaded and has no teardown entry point (none is specified).
The portable swizzle network is less efficient than a CPU-specific byte-shuffle
instruction. There is no dedicated pre-LLVM optimizing pass or bounds-check
elimination pass; LLVM performs ordinary promotion/inlining/optimization.

## Tests run

All execution comparisons below were run against `w2l-ref`, with generated code
compiled by LLVM 23 at **both `-O0` and `-O2`**:

* `cargo build --release --offline` and all **11** Rust unit tests pass.
* `tests/test.py`: **16 differential runs / 1,370 comparisons**, including all
  payloads' codec encode/decode workflows, packet bytes/final ranges, multi-value,
  control flow, bulk memory/table operations, host imports, traps, trap recovery,
  and malformed/invalid/out-of-scope rejection.
* `tests/scalar_matrix.py`: **41,966 commands per optimization level**, covering
  every scalar numeric opcode, NaNs, signed zeros, division overflow, shifts,
  and trapping/saturating conversion boundaries; no mismatches.
* `tests/simd_matrix.py`: **9,291 commands per optimization level**, covering
  every SIMD 1.0 opcode, lane endpoints, memory boundaries, arithmetic extremes,
  NaNs, and random vector bit patterns; no mismatches.
* `tests/smith.py`: **400 deterministic generated modules** translated, compiled,
  and differentially executed at both optimization levels. Unsupported features
  are explicitly disabled and reference loading checks the actual scope.
* `tests/recursion.py`: finite 10,000-frame calls, direct/mutual unbounded
  recursion trapping with code 8, and successful calls after traps all pass.
* `tests/stress.py`: **5,994,351-byte** synthetic module translated to
  20,273,963 bytes of LLVM IR in **0.265 seconds** in this environment.

An additional combined clean-CARGO_HOME/empty-environment/syscall-trace check

No hidden acceptance tests were available. See `tests/README.md` for commands.

# Local tests

All test programs are standard-library Python or C; external tools are used only
by tests, never by the translator.

```sh
cargo build --release --offline
cargo test --offline
python3 -I tests/test.py --no-build

mkdir -p tests/out
clang -std=c11 -O2 -rdynamic tests/harness.c -ldl -o tests/out/harness
python3 -I tests/scalar_matrix.py
python3 -I tests/simd_matrix.py tests/out/harness
python3 -I tests/recursion.py
python3 -I tests/smith.py --count 100
python3 -I tests/stress.py
```

`test.py` builds its own native driver and uses a temporary directory. Use
`--only control`, `--only bulk`, `--opt 0`, `--opt 2`, `--quick`, or `--keep`
to select work and preserve generated artifacts. The complete default run
includes all four payloads.

The other scripts preserve artifacts in ignored `tests/out/`. `smith.py` accepts
`--start N` and `--count N`; the recorded 400-module run used seeds 0 through 399.
Smith's unsupported features are explicitly disabled, and each generated module
is checked against the reference engine's scope before translation.

The C driver accepts the reference line protocol, with `.so` paths instead of
`.wasm` paths for `load`. It implements the provided imports and explicit trap
recovery. It does not install a native stack-overflow handler; recursion tests
use small frames and the translator's explicit depth trap.

Comparisons ignore unused ABI-slot bytes and allow NaN variation only for
arithmetic floating-point results. Integer results, bitwise operations, encoded
packets, and memory byte comparisons remain exact.
